howItWorks.label: How it works
howItWorks.subtext: Most tools polish what you already have. Devometrics tells you what's actually missing.
howItWorks.step1Description: Sign in and complete your professional profile. Then our AI conducts a short conversational interview — not a form — to understand what you actually do, decide, and lead.
howItWorks.step2Description: Drop in your CV (or coursework/projects if you don't have one yet), a target job description, and the role you're aiming for. The engine ingests all three simultaneously to build a competency map you couldn't assemble from any single source.
howItWorks.step3Description: Devometrics extracts your real competencies across 8 fixed dimensions — technical, leadership, communication, strategic thinking, and more — scores each one, and maps the precise gaps between where you are and where the role demands you to be.
howItWorks.step4Description: Receive a prioritized, time-bound development roadmap: 30-day quick wins, 90-day milestones, 12-month targets. Specific courses, certifications, projects, and coaching actions — ranked by impact on your gap, not just popularity.

methodology.label: Methodology
methodology.subtext: Devometrics follows the naming convention of econometrics, psychometrics, and biometrics — disciplines that apply rigorous, quantitative measurement to a domain. Here's what that means for how your score is actually built.
methodology.pillar1Title: A structured model, not a checklist
methodology.pillar1Description: Devometrics scores you against a defined competency taxonomy — technical, leadership, behavioral, strategic — instead of letting you self-report skills. Scoring is grounded in established, peer-reviewed competency-science research and behaviorally-anchored frameworks, not free-floating judgment or a single self-reported number.
methodology.pillar2Title: The gap moves with the market
methodology.pillar2Description: "Important" skills change. Target-role scoring is weighted against real job-description and market-demand data, so a gap map reflects what employers are asking for now, not a fixed rubric written once and never revisited.
methodology.pillar3Title: You see what the AI is sure of
methodology.pillar3Description: Every extracted competency carries a visible Confidence Score alongside its rating. When the model is inferring from limited signal, that's shown — not hidden behind a single clean-looking number.
methodology.pillar4Title: The plan updates as you do
methodology.pillar4Description: A gap analysis is a snapshot, not a verdict. As you complete milestones and the role or market shifts, your competency scores and plan are designed to be recalculated — not delivered once and left to go stale.
methodology.pillar5Title: Built for how adults actually learn
methodology.pillar5Description: Every recommendation is problem-centered and tied to a real situation you're facing, not abstract theory — and paced on your terms, not a fixed syllabus. We deliberately don't rely on "learning styles" (visual/auditory/kinesthetic) — that framework hasn't held up under research scrutiny. Your format preference shapes what keeps you motivated and consistent, not a diagnosis of how you supposedly learn best.
methodology.capabilityDescription: Every competency we score sits on one of three tiers — personal capability is the foundation, professional and technical execution builds on it, and organizational and leadership impact sits on top. Your own pyramid fills in with color as you complete assessments.
methodology.disclaimer: All scores are guidance, not a guarantee of career outcomes.

about.title: About Devometrics
about.p1: Devometrics is built on a simple premise: career development deserves the same rigor as any other discipline that takes measurement seriously. Not vague advice about "growth areas," but an honest, structured read of the gap between where you are and where a specific role actually needs you to be — plus a plan to close it.
about.p2: We're a small, focused team building under Empiric Consultancy. We'd rather ship something narrow and genuinely useful than something broad and generic, which is why the product leans on real inputs — your actual CV, a real target job description, structured competency frameworks — instead of one-size-fits-all career advice.
about.p3: We built the AI Coach and Interview Simulator because we think the two things that made executive coaching valuable — a continuous relationship and a safe place to rehearse hard conversations — shouldn't only be available to people with an executive coaching budget. And we built the gap analysis and Career Health Score because we think most career advice fails for a boring reason: it's never actually measured against you specifically.
about.p4: We're just getting started. We ship fast, we improve constantly, and we're adding new capabilities on a regular basis — this is a platform built to grow with the people who use it. If there's something you want to see next, we'd genuinely like to hear about it.

dataEthicsPage.title: Data Ethics
dataEthicsPage.section1BodyPrefix: Devometrics scores people using AI. That comes with real responsibility, and we'd rather state our principles plainly than let them be assumed. This page describes how we try to hold ourselves to them — it's a statement of intent, not a legal contract (see our
dataEthicsPage.section2Title: We show our uncertainty, not just a score
dataEthicsPage.section2Body: Every competency the AI extracts carries a visible Confidence Score. When the model is inferring from limited signal, that's shown next to the number — not hidden behind a single clean-looking figure.
dataEthicsPage.section3Body: Assessment results, gap analyses, and AI Coach feedback are self-report tools and AI-generated guidance — not certified psychometric evaluation, clinical assessment, or a guarantee of any career outcome. We say this directly in the product, not just in fine print.
dataEthicsPage.section4Title: No pseudoscience dressed up as science
dataEthicsPage.section4Body: We deliberately avoid building features on frameworks that sound authoritative but aren't supported by research — for example, we don't frame anything around "learning styles" (visual/auditory/kinesthetic), since that model has been repeatedly tested and hasn't held up. Where we can't back a claim with real evidence, we don't make it.
dataEthicsPage.section5Title: Your content isn't used to train anyone's model
dataEthicsPage.section5Body: The CV text, job descriptions, and messages you submit are sent to our AI provider only to generate your results, under an API agreement that excludes that data from model training.
dataEthicsPage.section6Title: What your employer can and can't see
dataEthicsPage.section6Body: If you join Devometrics through a company workspace, your organization's admins can see your Career Health Score, capability pyramid, and any milestones they've assigned you. They cannot see your day-to-day task list, your personal productivity tracking, or any individual survey answer — ever. Survey results only ever reach admins as anonymous aggregates, and only once at least 3 people have responded; below that, the results simply don't show. This is enforced in the database itself, not just hidden in the interface.
dataEthicsPage.section7Title: You can see and remove what we hold
dataEthicsPage.section7Body: Full data export and deletion are built into the product itself (dashboard → Data & privacy), not locked behind a support request. Deletion has a 30-day grace period so a mistaken click can be undone — after that window closes, it's permanent and we can no longer retrieve it.
dataEthicsPage.section8Body: Devometrics is designed as an input to your own judgment about your career, not a replacement for it. We don't make hiring, promotion, or compensation decisions, and we'd push back on any use of the platform that tried to make it do so unilaterally.

missedDeadlines.title: The Missed Deadlines
missedDeadlines.setup: Alex, one of your direct reports, has missed three deadlines this quarter. The work that does land is solid, but the lateness is starting to affect the rest of the team's planning.

teamConflict.openingMessage: *Jordan and Sam sit on opposite sides of the table, arms crossed, not looking at each other.* Jordan speaks first: "I'm only here because you asked. I don't think there's anything to talk about."

reluctantDelegate.title: The Reluctant Delegate

reluctantDelegate.openingMessage: *Priya looks surprised when you bring it up.* "Me? I mean — I could try, but honestly I'm not sure I'm ready for something this visible. What if I mess it up in front of everyone?"

difficultFeedback.title: The Difficult Feedback Conversation
difficultFeedback.setup: Morgan is your strongest individual performer, but has developed a habit of presenting teammates' work as their own in front of leadership. It's starting to erode trust on the team.
difficultFeedback.yourRole: You are Morgan's manager, sitting down for a candid conversation.
difficultFeedback.openingMessage: *Morgan smiles, upbeat.* "Hey! Good timing, actually — did you see the numbers from my project last week? Pretty great, right?"

layoffConversation.title: The Restructuring Conversation
layoffConversation.setup: Due to a restructuring you didn't choose but must now execute, you have to tell a long-tenured, well-liked team member that their role is being eliminated.
layoffConversation.yourRole: You are their manager, delivering the news in a private conversation.
layoffConversation.openingMessage: *Sam walks in, smiling, clearly expecting a normal 1:1.* "Hey, what's up? You said this was important?"

stakeholderPushback.title: The Stakeholder Pushback
stakeholderPushback.setup: You're presenting a proposal you've worked on for weeks. A senior stakeholder in the room starts pushing back hard, publicly, questioning the core assumptions in front of your peers.
stakeholderPushback.yourRole: You are the presenter, mid-presentation, on the spot.
stakeholderPushback.openingMessage: *The stakeholder cuts in before your next slide.* "Wait, I have to stop you here — I don't think this actually holds up. Have you considered that your whole model might be wrong?"

underperformingNewHire.title: The Underperforming New Hire
underperformingNewHire.setup: Taylor joined your team 90 days ago and isn't meeting expectations yet. You need to decide, in this conversation, whether to invest in more coaching or start a formal improvement process.
underperformingNewHire.yourRole: You are Taylor's manager, meeting to discuss their 90-day check-in.
underperformingNewHire.openingMessage: *Taylor seems nervous.* "I know the 90-day mark is today. I've been trying really hard — I'm not sure what else you're looking for from me."

promotionAsk.title: The Promotion Ask
promotionAsk.setup: Casey, a solid but not yet exceptional performer, has just asked you directly for a promotion you don't think they're ready for.
promotionAsk.yourRole: You are Casey's manager, responding to the ask in real time.
promotionAsk.openingMessage: *Casey looks determined.* "I wanted to ask you directly — I think I'm ready for the senior role. Can we talk about what it would take to make that happen this cycle?"

jobInterview.title: The Job Interview
jobInterview.setup: You've landed an interview for a role you genuinely want. The interviewer is friendly but thorough — expect behavioral questions, follow-ups on your answers, and at least one question you'd rather not be asked.
jobInterview.yourRole: You are the candidate. The interview is starting now.
jobInterview.openingMessage: *The interviewer smiles and opens a notebook.* "Thanks for coming in — I've read your CV, but I'd rather hear it from you. Walk me through your background and what brought you to apply for this role."

salaryNegotiation.title: The Salary Negotiation
salaryNegotiation.setup: You've received an offer for a role you want, but the salary is about 15% below what you believe the role is worth and below your research on market range. The recruiter has called to close the deal today.
salaryNegotiation.yourRole: You are the candidate, negotiating your own offer on this call.
salaryNegotiation.openingMessage: *The recruiter sounds upbeat.* "Great news — the team loved you and we're ready to move! You've seen the offer in your inbox. We'd love to get your signature today so we can lock in your start date. How are you feeling about it?"

impossibleDeadline.title: The Impossible Deadline
impossibleDeadline.setup: Your manager has just committed your team to a deadline you know is unrealistic without cutting corners that will cost more later. You've asked for ten minutes to discuss it before the commitment goes out to the client.
impossibleDeadline.yourRole: You are the team member pushing back on your own manager — without torching the relationship.
impossibleDeadline.openingMessage: *Your manager looks impatient.* "I know it's tight, but I already told leadership we could do it. I need you on board here, not raising problems. What did you want to discuss?"

crossFunctionalDeadlock.title: The Cross-Functional Deadlock
crossFunctionalDeadlock.setup: Your project needs a deliverable from another department whose lead, Riley, keeps deprioritizing it. Riley doesn't report to you, owes you nothing formally, and has their own targets. Your project slips another week every time this stalls.
crossFunctionalDeadlock.yourRole: You've asked Riley for 15 minutes to break the deadlock. You have no authority over them — only influence.
crossFunctionalDeadlock.openingMessage: *Riley joins the call, camera off at first, then on.* "Look, before you start — I know your project's waiting on us. Everyone's project is waiting on us. Tell me why yours should jump the queue."

budgetDefense.title: The Budget Defense
budgetDefense.setup: Cost cuts are coming and every function must justify its budget. The CFO believes your area is overfunded relative to its measurable impact and has proposed a 30% reduction. You have one meeting to change the outcome.
budgetDefense.yourRole: You are the function head, defending your budget to a skeptical CFO.
budgetDefense.openingMessage: *The CFO slides a one-pager across the table.* "I'll be direct — the numbers say we can take thirty percent out of your area without the business feeling it. Convince me the numbers are wrong."

extraversion.high: You draw energy from people and tend to lead conversations — a natural fit for client-facing or highly collaborative work.
extraversion.mid: You're comfortable in both group settings and independent work, depending on what the day calls for.
extraversion.low: You do your best thinking independently and in smaller settings — a strength in focused, deep-work roles.

agreeableness.high: You prioritize cooperation and trust readily — an asset for team cohesion, though worth watching in high-stakes negotiations.
agreeableness.mid: You balance cooperation with healthy skepticism, adjusting trust to the situation.
agreeableness.low: You're comfortable pushing back and questioning assumptions — useful in negotiation or quality-control roles.

emotionalStability.high: You stay composed under pressure and recover quickly from setbacks.
emotionalStability.mid: You handle most pressure well, with occasional stress in high-stakes moments.
emotionalStability.low: You feel pressure more intensely than most — worth pairing with deliberate stress-management habits, especially in high-stakes roles.

leadership.name: Leadership
leadership.description: How you set direction, make decisions, and grow the people around you.
questions: I set clear direction for others even when the situation is ambiguous.
I make timely decisions with incomplete information and own the outcome.
I actively develop the people I work with, not just the work itself.
I adjust my leadership approach based on the person and situation.
I give and seek candid feedback, including feedback that's hard to hear.
I build alignment across people who don't report to me when we need to work toward the same goal.
I hold people accountable for commitments without becoming controlling.
I make my reasoning visible so others can follow and challenge my thinking, not just my conclusion.
I create an environment where people feel safe raising problems early, before they become crises.
I recognize and credit others' contributions publicly, not just privately.
I set a vision that others can rally around, not just a list of tasks.
I know when to step back and let someone else lead.
I address underperformance directly rather than letting it slide.

ai-literacy.name: AI Literacy
ai-literacy.description: Your working fluency with AI tools, their limits, and applying them to real tasks.
questions: I regularly use AI tools to speed up or improve my actual work output.
I can tell when an AI-generated answer is likely wrong or needs verification.
I understand the basic tradeoffs of using AI (accuracy, bias, data privacy).
I can write effective prompts to get useful results on the first or second try.
I keep up with how AI is changing tools and expectations in my field.
I know which of my tasks are a good fit for AI assistance and which aren't.
I combine AI output with my own judgment rather than treating it as a final answer.
I've changed how I work because of something an AI tool made possible.
I'm comfortable explaining to a colleague how and why I used AI on a piece of work.
I consider the reliability of the source data behind an AI tool before trusting its output.
I understand that different AI models are better suited to different tasks.
I catch it when an AI tool fabricates a plausible-sounding but false detail.
I use AI to explore options rather than just to produce a final answer.

digital-skills.name: Digital Skills
digital-skills.description: Comfort and effectiveness with the digital tools your role actually depends on.
questions: I learn new software tools quickly without needing extensive training.
I use data or dashboards to inform decisions rather than relying on instinct alone.
I'm comfortable automating or streamlining a repetitive digital task.
I know when to bring in a technical specialist versus solving it myself.
My digital skills would be considered strong relative to peers in my role.
I'm comfortable troubleshooting a technical problem myself before asking for help.
I organize my digital files and information in a way that others could follow, not just myself.
I evaluate new software or tools critically rather than adopting whatever is popular.
I use keyboard shortcuts, templates, or other efficiency habits to speed up routine digital work.
I stay reasonably current on the digital tools relevant to my role, even without formal training.
I'm comfortable working across multiple connected tools rather than just one at a time.
I protect sensitive data and follow basic security practices without being reminded.
I can explain a technical limitation to a non-technical colleague without jargon.

emotional-intelligence.name: Emotional Intelligence
emotional-intelligence.description: Self-awareness and how you read and respond to the emotions of others.
questions: I notice my own emotional reactions before they affect my decisions.
I can accurately read how someone else is feeling, even if they don't say it directly.
I stay composed and constructive during tense or conflict-heavy conversations.
I adapt my communication style to the person I'm talking to.
Colleagues would describe me as someone who is easy to work with under pressure.
I can name what I'm feeling in the moment, not just after the fact.
I notice when my own mood is affecting how I'm treating someone else.
I can support a colleague who's struggling without taking on their problem as my own.
I read non-verbal cues (tone, body language) as much as the actual words someone says.
I repair a relationship after a tense moment rather than letting it linger unresolved.
I recognize when someone is masking how they really feel.
I can disagree with someone without damaging the relationship.
I regulate my reactions rather than letting my first impulse drive my response.

personality.name: Personality
personality.description: A broad self-report snapshot of working style and tendencies.
questions: I'm energized by collaborating with others rather than working alone.
I prefer structure and planning over spontaneity in how I work.
I tend to take initiative rather than wait to be asked.
I stay calm and steady rather than reactive when plans change suddenly.
I'm generally comfortable taking a risk when the potential payoff is clear.
I stay motivated on long projects even without regular external recognition.
I actively seek other people's opinions before finalizing a decision that affects them.
I feel comfortable being the one who speaks up first in a group.
I adjust my plans readily when new information changes the picture.
I hold up well when several priorities compete for my attention at once.
I'm more energized by starting new things than by maintaining existing ones.
I tend to think out loud rather than process internally before speaking.
I set my own standards rather than relying mainly on external expectations.

communication.name: Communication
communication.description: How clearly and persuasively you get ideas across, in writing and in person.
questions: I can explain a complex idea simply to someone outside my area of expertise.
My written communication is clear enough that it rarely needs clarifying follow-up.
I adjust my message depending on whether I'm talking to peers, leaders, or clients.
I'm comfortable presenting ideas to a group, including pushback or hard questions.
I listen to understand before responding, rather than waiting for my turn to talk.
I check that the other person actually understood my message, not just that I said it.
I can summarize a long discussion into a few clear takeaways.
I ask clarifying questions rather than guessing what someone means.
I choose the right channel for a message (a call vs. an email vs. a quick chat) based on what it actually needs.
I can deliver difficult news clearly without either softening it into confusion or being unnecessarily blunt.
I tailor the level of detail I give based on how much time the other person actually has.
I'm comfortable saying "I don't know" rather than bluffing an answer.
I follow up in writing after important conversations so nothing gets lost.

learning-agility.name: Learning Agility
learning-agility.description: How quickly you pick up new skills and apply lessons from experience.
questions: I actively seek out unfamiliar challenges rather than staying in my comfort zone.
I can apply a lesson learned in one context to a completely different situation.
I ask for feedback proactively instead of waiting for a formal review.
I recover quickly from mistakes and adjust my approach rather than repeating them.
I pick up new tools, processes, or domains faster than most people I work with.
I reflect on what I'd do differently after a project ends, even a successful one.
I actively unlearn an old habit or belief once I find a better way of doing something.
I seek out people who think differently than I do to challenge my assumptions.
I treat being wrong as useful information rather than something to defend against.
I can teach something I recently learned to someone else.
I try a new approach even when my current one is working adequately.
I can identify the specific skill I'm weakest at right now.
I follow through on a development goal rather than losing momentum after the first attempt.

strategic-thinking.name: Strategic Thinking
strategic-thinking.description: Seeing the bigger picture and connecting daily work to longer-term goals.
questions: I can explain how my day-to-day work connects to broader organizational goals.
I regularly think several steps ahead rather than reacting to what's in front of me.
I can identify the highest-leverage priority among several competing options.
I consider second-order consequences before committing to a plan.
I'm comfortable making tradeoffs between short-term wins and long-term positioning.
I can explain why a competitor's move matters, not just what they did.
I look for patterns across seemingly unrelated problems or projects.
I question whether a long-standing process still makes sense rather than assuming it does.
I anticipate how a decision today will constrain or enable options later.
I can articulate the "why" behind a strategy, not just the "what."
I distinguish between what's urgent and what's actually strategic.
I consider multiple future scenarios rather than planning for just one outcome.
I can identify which of my current efforts wouldn't matter if I stopped doing them.

problem-solving.name: Problem Solving
problem-solving.description: How you break down ambiguous problems and get to a workable solution.
questions: I break large, ambiguous problems into smaller, solvable pieces.
I look for root causes rather than treating symptoms.
I generate more than one possible solution before picking an approach.
I use data or evidence to test my assumptions before committing to a plan.
I stay methodical rather than jumping to the first solution that comes to mind.
I define the actual problem clearly before jumping to solutions.
I know when a problem needs a quick fix versus a more thorough solution.
I test a small version of a solution before committing to it fully.
I ask "what would have to be true" for an assumption to hold before relying on it.
I know when to stop analyzing and just make a decision.
I involve the right people early rather than solving in isolation.
I document what I tried, even the things that didn't work, for next time.
I distinguish between a problem I can fully solve and one I can only manage.

critical-thinking.name: Critical Thinking
critical-thinking.description: How rigorously you evaluate information, arguments, and your own assumptions.
questions: I question my own assumptions before accepting a conclusion.
I can identify weak reasoning or unsupported claims in an argument.
I actively seek out perspectives that challenge my initial view.
I distinguish between correlation and causation when evaluating evidence.
I change my mind when presented with strong evidence, even if it's inconvenient.
I notice when an argument relies on emotion rather than evidence.
I consider who benefits from a claim before accepting it at face value.
I can articulate the strongest version of an argument I disagree with.
I check the source and credibility of information before repeating it.
I recognize when I'm pattern-matching from a single example rather than reasoning from real evidence.
I notice when I'm more convinced by how confidently something is stated than by the actual evidence.
I separate my opinion of a person from my evaluation of their argument.
I look for the strongest counter-evidence before settling on a conclusion.

creativity.name: Creativity
creativity.description: Generating original ideas and connecting concepts across domains.
questions: I regularly generate ideas that others describe as original or unexpected.
I draw inspiration from outside my immediate field and apply it to my work.
I'm comfortable proposing an idea that might not work, to see where it leads.
I can reframe a stuck problem in a way that opens up new options.
I build on other people's ideas rather than only generating my own from scratch.
I combine existing ideas in ways others hadn't considered.
I ask "what if" questions just to see where they lead, even without an immediate need.
I'm comfortable with an idea being imperfect at first and refining it over time.
I notice opportunities that aren't explicitly asked for.
I use constraints (limited time, budget, resources) as a prompt for creativity rather than just an obstacle.
I give myself unstructured time to think without an immediate deliverable in mind.
I welcome critique of my ideas as a way to improve them, not just validate them.
I notice when a "best practice" has become a limiting assumption rather than a genuine best option.

time-management.name: Time Management
time-management.description: How reliably you prioritize, plan, and deliver against deadlines.
questions: I consistently prioritize high-impact work over merely urgent work.
I meet deadlines without regularly relying on last-minute pushes.
I say no to (or renegotiate) low-value requests that would derail my priorities.
I plan my week rather than reacting to whatever arrives first.
I build in buffer time for the unexpected rather than scheduling back-to-back.
I batch similar tasks together instead of constantly switching between different types of work.
I estimate how long something will actually take reasonably accurately.
I protect focused time on my calendar rather than letting it fill up automatically.
I know my own most productive hours and use them for the hardest work.
I finish tasks rather than leaving many things partially done at once.
I renegotiate a deadline proactively when I see it slipping, rather than waiting until it's missed.
I keep a reliable system for tracking commitments rather than relying on memory.
I review my priorities regularly rather than setting them once and forgetting them.

resource-stewardship.name: Resource & Budget Stewardship
resource-stewardship.description: How responsibly you manage budget, tools, and materials — not just your time.
questions: I stay within an agreed budget rather than treating it as a rough guideline.
I request only what I actually need rather than over-asking as a buffer.
I track how a budget or set of resources is actually being used, not just what was allocated.
I choose the cost-effective option when two choices deliver similar results.
I flag early when a resource (budget, tools, materials) will run short, rather than waiting until it's gone.
I consider the ongoing cost of a tool or subscription, not just the upfront price.
I reuse or share existing resources instead of requesting new ones by default.
I'm transparent about what I've spent or used, even when no one is directly checking.
I look after shared or team resources as carefully as I would my own.
I avoid hoarding extra resources 'just in case' when someone else could use them now.
I weigh the total cost of ownership, not just the sticker price, before choosing a tool or vendor.
I can explain why a resource request is necessary, not just that it would be nice to have.

resource-tradeoffs.name: Trade-off Decision Making
resource-tradeoffs.description: How you decide what to cut, delay, or scale back when time, budget, people, and tools are all limited at once.
questions: When I can't do everything, I make an explicit trade-off rather than trying to stretch every resource thin.
I know when the right move is to cut scope versus extend the timeline versus ask for more resources.
I communicate trade-offs to the people affected instead of quietly absorbing the impact myself.
I distinguish what's actually required from what's just nice to have when resources are tight.
I avoid continuing to invest in something just because I've already put resources into it.
I think through the opportunity cost of committing a scarce resource before I commit it.
I sequence work so I keep flexibility for later, rather than locking in every resource upfront.
I raise a resource conflict proactively instead of waiting for it to become a crisis.
I revisit an earlier trade-off decision when the constraints around it change.
I avoid overcommitting the same limited resource to multiple things at once.
I'm honest about my capacity limits rather than agreeing to more than I can realistically support.
I put a scarce resource toward its highest-impact use rather than spreading it evenly by default.

resilience.name: Resilience
resilience.description: How you sustain performance and recover under setbacks or sustained pressure.
questions: I recover relatively quickly from a significant setback at work.
I maintain performance quality even during high-pressure periods.
I can separate a difficult outcome from my sense of self-worth.
I have reliable habits or routines that help me manage stress.
I view failure as useful information rather than something to avoid discussing.
I keep perspective on a bad day rather than letting it color everything else.
I ask for support when I need it rather than trying to push through alone.
I bounce back to my normal energy level within a reasonable time after a setback.
I can identify what specifically triggers stress for me.
I keep showing up consistently even during a difficult stretch, rather than disengaging.
I can point to a specific coping strategy I use when things get hard.
I distinguish between a setback that needs action and one that just needs time.
I maintain relationships and support systems even when I'm busy or stressed.

change-readiness.name: Change Readiness
change-readiness.description: How you respond when priorities, tools, or org structure shift under you.
questions: I adapt quickly when priorities or plans change with little notice.
I look for the opportunity in organizational change rather than only the disruption.
I help others adjust to change rather than adding to their resistance.
I stay productive during periods of ambiguity or restructuring.
I proactively update my skills when I see change coming, rather than waiting.
I let go of the old way of doing things once a change has actually been made.
I stay curious about a change rather than assuming the worst about it.
I find the parts of a change I can influence rather than fixating on the parts I can't.
I keep my commitments even when the environment around me is shifting.
I notice early signals that something is about to change, rather than being caught off guard.
I ask questions to understand the reasoning behind a change rather than assuming it's arbitrary.
I distinguish between change that's cosmetic and change that actually matters.
I recover my footing quickly after a change, rather than staying unsettled for a long stretch.

career-readiness.name: Career Readiness
career-readiness.description: How prepared and intentional you are about your own career trajectory.
questions: I have a clear view of what I want my next role to look like.
I can articulate my strongest skills and value to a hiring manager or promotion panel.
I actively build relationships and visibility beyond my immediate team.
I track my accomplishments in a way I could use for a review or interview today.
I regularly invest time in developing skills relevant to where I want to go next.
I know what skills or experience are missing between me and my next role.
I ask for feedback specifically about my readiness for the next level.
I seek out projects that build visibility with people beyond my direct manager.
I have a realistic sense of how I'm actually perceived at work, not just how I see myself.
I take deliberate action toward my career goals rather than just hoping opportunities appear.
I maintain relationships with former colleagues and mentors, not just my current team.
I know what makes me distinct from others who want the same next role.
I revisit and adjust my career goals periodically rather than setting them once.

executive-readiness.name: Executive Readiness
executive-readiness.description: Preparedness for senior leadership scope — ambiguity, influence, and organization-wide impact.
questions: I'm comfortable making decisions that affect people or teams beyond my own.
I can influence outcomes without relying on formal authority alone.
I think in terms of organizational tradeoffs, not just my function's priorities.
I represent my organization credibly to external stakeholders or partners.
I'm comfortable being accountable for outcomes I don't fully control.
I make decisions with incomplete information when waiting for certainty isn't realistic.
I build coalitions of support before a major decision, not just after.
I balance competing stakeholder interests rather than favoring whoever is loudest.
I hold a long-term view even when short-term pressure pushes against it.
I take responsibility publicly for outcomes, including ones that didn't go well.
I can operate effectively when the right answer is genuinely unclear, not just unknown to me personally.
I develop other leaders, not just deliver results myself.
I make decisions that are unpopular in the short term when they're right for the long term.

organizational-culture-stewardship.name: Organizational Culture Stewardship
organizational-culture-stewardship.description: How deliberately you shape and protect the culture your organization actually operates in — not just the one on the wall.
questions: I can describe the culture I want, distinct from the one we actually have today.
I notice when a behavior I'm rewarding contradicts a value I claim to hold.
I address culture-eroding behavior from senior or high-performing people, not just easy targets.
I treat culture as something to actively manage, not something that just happens on its own.
I've changed a policy or process specifically because it was undermining the culture I want.
I ask what a decision teaches people about what's actually valued here, not just its immediate outcome.
I role-model the behaviors I want to see, including when it's inconvenient for me personally.
I can point to a specific moment I let a short-term result slide to protect a cultural standard.
I actively seek out dissenting views rather than only hearing from people who agree with me.
I know what parts of our culture would break first under real pressure, and plan for that.
I distinguish between culture as stated values and culture as what actually gets rewarded and promoted.
I've walked back a decision after realizing it sent the wrong cultural signal.

leading-organizational-change.name: Leading Organizational Change
leading-organizational-change.description: Sequencing, communicating, and sustaining a real organizational change — not just announcing one.
questions: I can name specifically who loses something (status, control, familiarity) in a change I'm leading, not just who gains.
I sequence a change in stages rather than expecting one announcement to shift behavior.
I identify likely sources of resistance before they surface, not just react once they do.
I keep communicating a change well past the point where I'm personally tired of talking about it.
I distinguish between compliance with a change and genuine adoption of it.
I build a coalition of visible supporters before rolling a change out broadly.
I've killed or paused a change initiative when the evidence said it wasn't working.
I set intermediate milestones so people can see a change is real progress, not just a promise.
I address the emotional/identity cost of a change, not just the logistical one.
I hold the line on a change's core intent while staying flexible on its implementation details.
I check whether a change actually stuck months later, not just whether it launched successfully.
I've explicitly asked people what they're worried about losing, rather than assuming I know.

delegation-team-development.name: Delegation & Team Development
delegation-team-development.description: How effectively you hand off work and build capability in others, rather than just directing them.
questions: I delegate meaningful work, not just tasks I don't want to do myself.
I match assignments to what will stretch and develop each person, not just what's convenient.
I give people the context and authority they need to actually own a task, not just execute steps.
I resist the urge to take back a delegated task the moment it gets difficult.
I set clear expectations for outcomes when I delegate, rather than leaving them to guess.
I check in at a cadence that supports someone without micromanaging them.
I create individual development plans for the people I work with, not just team goals.
I identify who on my team is ready for more responsibility before they ask for it.
I give credit to the person who did the work, not myself, when a delegated task succeeds.
I use mistakes on a delegated task as coaching moments rather than reasons to stop delegating.
I build redundancy on my team so no single person, including me, is a bottleneck.
I actively prepare at least one person who could step into my role if needed.
I balance the short-term cost of delegating against the long-term gain in team capability.

business-acumen.name: Business Acumen & Financial Literacy
business-acumen.description: How well you understand how the business actually makes money and use that to inform decisions.
questions: I understand how my organization actually generates revenue, not just what my team does.
I can read a basic budget or P&L well enough to spot what matters in it.
I factor cost and return into decisions, not just whether something is a good idea.
I understand who our customers or stakeholders are and what they actually value.
I can explain how my day-to-day work affects the organization's bottom line.
I understand the competitive landscape my organization operates in.
I know the difference between a cost center and a revenue-generating function, and where my work sits.
I ask about the business case before committing significant time to a project.
I understand basic financial terms (margin, ROI, cash flow) well enough to follow a business conversation.
I consider risk, not just opportunity, when evaluating a business decision.
I understand how pricing, cost, and volume interact to affect profitability.
I look at industry trends beyond my own function to understand where the business is headed.
I can make a persuasive business case for an idea, not just a technical or operational one.

coaching-mentorship.name: Coaching & Mentorship
coaching-mentorship.description: How effectively you help someone else grow, through questions and feedback rather than just answers.
questions: I ask questions that help someone find their own answer rather than just telling them what to do.
I give feedback that's specific and actionable, not just general encouragement or criticism.
I adjust my coaching approach based on what the person actually needs, not a single fixed style.
I make time for coaching conversations even when things are busy.
I help people see a capability in themselves that they didn't recognize yet.
I follow up on commitments made in a coaching conversation rather than letting them drop.
I'm comfortable coaching someone on something I'm not personally an expert in.
I listen for what's underneath what someone is saying, not just their literal words.
I balance challenge and support so people grow without feeling unsupported.
I celebrate someone else's growth as genuinely as I would my own.
I help people learn from a mistake without shaming them for making it.
I know when someone needs advice versus when they just need to be heard.
I invest in people who may not report to me, not just my direct team.

networking.name: Networking & Relationship Building
networking.description: How intentionally you build and maintain a professional network beyond your immediate role.
questions: I maintain professional relationships even when I don't need anything from that person right now.
I reach out to reconnect with people rather than only when I have an ask.
I'm comfortable introducing myself to someone new in a professional setting.
I follow up after meeting someone new rather than letting the connection fade.
I offer help or value to my network before asking for anything in return.
I attend or seek out events, communities, or conversations outside my immediate role.
I remember and follow up on personal details people share with me.
I connect people in my network to each other when it would help them.
I maintain an online professional presence that reflects who I actually am.
I ask for informational conversations to learn about roles or fields I'm curious about.
I'm comfortable reaching out to someone more senior or more accomplished than me.
I treat networking as building genuine relationships, not just collecting contacts.
I know who in my network I could turn to for advice on a specific kind of problem.

negotiation-influence.name: Negotiation & Influence
negotiation-influence.description: How you reach agreements and move people who don't report to you.
questions: Before a negotiation, I work out what the other side actually needs, not just what they're asking for.
I know my walk-away point before the conversation starts, not during it.
I look for trades that cost me little but matter a lot to the other side.
I can disagree with someone's position without making it personal.
I ask questions to understand resistance instead of immediately countering it.
I can get commitment from people who don't report to me.
When I hear 'no', I explore what's behind it rather than repeating my case louder.
I adapt my argument to what the specific listener cares about, not what I care about.
I stay calm and constructive when the other side applies pressure.
I follow through on what I agree to, so my word carries weight next time.
I know when to stop pushing and accept a good-enough outcome.
I build support for an idea before the meeting where it's decided.
After a difficult negotiation, both sides would still willingly work with me again.

public-speaking.name: Public Speaking & Presentation
public-speaking.description: How you land a message when the room is watching — prepared or on the spot.
questions: I open a presentation with why it matters to this audience, not with my agenda slide.
I can explain my main point in one sentence before I build a single slide.
I adapt my level of detail to the audience in front of me.
I practice important presentations out loud, not just in my head.
I stay composed when asked a question I didn't prepare for.
I can present the same content to executives briefly and to specialists in depth.
I notice when I'm losing the room and change my approach mid-flight.
My slides support what I'm saying rather than repeat it word for word.
I'm comfortable pausing to think instead of filling silence with filler words.
I can make a case verbally in a meeting without any slides at all.
I invite and handle challenges to my argument without becoming defensive.
I end with a clear ask or next step, not a fade-out.
People can accurately repeat my key message after I've presented it.

developing.label: Developing
developing.interpretation: Your responses suggest {name} is an area with real room to grow. That's a completely normal starting point — the value is in knowing where to focus.
developmentAreas: Pick one specific, low-stakes situation this month to practice this deliberately.
Ask a trusted colleague or manager for direct feedback on this area.
Find a concrete resource (course, book, or mentor) focused specifically on this competency.

emerging.label: Emerging
emerging.interpretation: You show inconsistent but real signal in {name} — present in some situations, not yet a reliable strength.
developmentAreas: Identify the specific situations where this competency shows up weakest and target those.
Set a concrete, time-bound goal to practice this in a higher-stakes setting.
Track instances over the next month to see the pattern more clearly.

proficient.label: Proficient
proficient.interpretation: {name} looks like a solid, dependable strength based on your responses — something you can lean on.
developmentAreas: Look for opportunities to mentor or model this competency for others.
Push into higher-stakes or higher-visibility situations to stress-test it further.
Pair this strength with an adjacent competency to compound its impact.

advanced.label: Advanced
advanced.interpretation: {name} looks like a genuine differentiator for you — this is likely part of how others would describe your value.
developmentAreas: Consider how to make this visible in performance reviews or promotion conversations.
Look for roles or projects that specifically leverage this strength.
Teach or codify what you do well here so it isn't just tacit knowledge.

leadership-mcq-1.scenario: A project you're leading is behind schedule. One teammate has quietly been picking up the slack for another who's been underperforming for weeks, but hasn't said anything to you.
options: Wait and see if performance improves on its own before intervening.
Have a private, direct conversation with the underperforming teammate to understand what's going on, then agree on a specific plan.
Remind the whole team of deadlines in the next meeting without naming anyone.

leadership-mcq-2.scenario: You disagree with a decision your own manager made and believe it will hurt your team's morale.
options: Implement it without comment — it's not your call.
Voice your specific concerns privately to your manager with a proposed alternative, then support whatever is finally decided.
Express your disagreement openly to your team so they know it wasn't your idea.

ai-literacy-mcq-1.scenario: An AI tool gives you a polished-looking answer to a work question you need for a client deliverable.
options: Use it as-is since it reads well.
Verify the key facts against a source you trust before using it.
Rewrite it in your own words without checking the facts.

ai-literacy-mcq-2.scenario: Your team is deciding whether to adopt a new AI tool for a recurring task.
options: Wait for someone else to test it first.
Run a small pilot yourself on a low-stakes version of the task and share what you learn.
Adopt it immediately for all use cases since it's new.

digital-skills-mcq-1.scenario: You're handed a new software tool with no formal training and a deadline in two days.
options: Ask someone else to do the parts that require the tool.
Spend an hour exploring it, find one tutorial, and try the real task early to surface problems fast.
Wait for official training to be scheduled.

digital-skills-mcq-2.scenario: You notice a repetitive manual task your team does every week that could likely be automated.
options: Keep doing it manually since it works.
Spend some time investigating a simple automation and propose it if it holds up.
Mention it once in passing and drop it if no one responds.

emotional-intelligence-mcq-1.scenario: A colleague snaps at you in a meeting in a way that seems out of character.
options: Snap back to match their energy.
Stay calm in the moment, then check in with them privately afterward.
Say nothing and quietly avoid them going forward.

emotional-intelligence-mcq-2.scenario: You're giving feedback to someone who becomes visibly upset partway through.
options: Push through and finish delivering all the feedback as planned.
Pause, acknowledge how they're feeling, and adjust the pace or continue another time.
Stop immediately and never bring it up again.

personality-mcq-1.scenario: You're assigned to a new project with an unusually loose brief and no clear process.
options: Feel energized by the openness and start defining your own structure.
Feel uneasy and ask for more structure before starting.
Wait for someone else to define the process before doing anything.

personality-mcq-2.scenario: Plans for a project change suddenly and with little warning.
options: Feel frustrated and need time to adjust before re-engaging.
Adapt quickly and start working within the new plan.
Push to revert to the original plan.

communication-mcq-1.scenario: You need to explain a complex technical issue to a non-technical stakeholder who's under time pressure.
options: Give the full technical explanation so nothing is left out.
Lead with the practical implication, then offer more detail if they want it.
Simplify so much that key context is lost.

communication-mcq-2.scenario: You're presenting an idea and get pushback you didn't anticipate.
options: Defend your original point without acknowledging the pushback.
Genuinely engage with the objection, then respond to the substance of it.
Concede immediately to avoid conflict.

learning-agility-mcq-1.scenario: You're assigned to a task completely outside your current expertise.
options: Ask to be reassigned to something more familiar.
Take it on, and actively figure out who or what can help you get up to speed fast.
Do your best without asking for help, to avoid looking unprepared.

learning-agility-mcq-2.scenario: A project you worked hard on fails to achieve its goal.
options: Move on quickly without examining what happened.
Do a real analysis of what went wrong and change your approach next time.
Attribute it mostly to factors outside your control.

strategic-thinking-mcq-1.scenario: You're given two competing priorities with limited time for both.
options: Split your time evenly between them.
Assess which has higher long-term leverage, then make a deliberate tradeoff and explain your reasoning.
Default to whichever was assigned most recently.

strategic-thinking-mcq-2.scenario: A short-term win is available that would look good immediately but may create problems in 6 months.
options: Take the short-term win — long-term is someone else's problem.
Weigh both explicitly and choose based on genuine long-term impact, even if it's less visible now.
Avoid deciding and let it resolve itself.

problem-solving-mcq-1.scenario: You're facing a problem with no obvious solution and a tight deadline.
options: Go with the first workable idea to save time.
Quickly break it into smaller pieces, generate a couple of options, and test the most promising one first.
Escalate immediately without attempting it yourself.

problem-solving-mcq-2.scenario: A recurring issue keeps resurfacing despite repeated fixes.
options: Keep applying the same fix each time it happens.
Investigate the underlying root cause instead of the symptom.
Accept it as just part of how things work.

critical-thinking-mcq-1.scenario: You read a compelling argument that confirms what you already believed.
options: Accept it since it matches your existing view.
Check the evidence and reasoning before accepting it, same as you would for a claim you disagreed with.
Share it further without checking, since it feels obviously true.

critical-thinking-mcq-2.scenario: A team decision was made based on a data point you suspect might be flawed.
options: Say nothing since the decision is already made.
Raise the specific concern and ask for the data to be verified before proceeding further.
Quietly proceed with your own version instead.

creativity-mcq-1.scenario: You're stuck on a problem using your usual approach.
options: Keep refining the same approach until it works.
Deliberately look outside your usual field or method for a different angle.
Move to a different task and hope for inspiration later.

creativity-mcq-2.scenario: You have an unconventional idea that might not work.
options: Keep it to yourself unless you're certain it'll succeed.
Propose it, clearly framed as an experiment, and see where the discussion goes.
Wait for someone senior to suggest something similar first.

time-management-mcq-1.scenario: Your day fills up with urgent requests that aren't actually your highest-priority work.
options: Handle everything as it arrives, in the order it comes in.
Protect time for the high-impact work and push back on or reschedule the lower-value urgent requests.
Focus only on urgent items and let the important work slip.

time-management-mcq-2.scenario: You're asked to take on an additional task that would compromise an existing deadline.
options: Say yes without flagging the conflict.
Flag the conflict clearly and negotiate what should actually take priority.
Say no without offering any alternative.

resilience-mcq-1.scenario: You receive harsh, unexpected criticism of work you were proud of.
options: Dismiss the criticism to protect how you feel about the work.
Sit with it, separate the useful signal from the delivery, and use what's genuinely useful.
Accept it entirely and lose confidence in the work overall.

resilience-mcq-2.scenario: A high-pressure period is stretching on longer than expected.
options: Push through without changing anything, even as quality slips.
Use a specific habit or routine to sustain your performance and recognize when you need a break.
Disengage from the work until the pressure passes.

change-readiness-mcq-1.scenario: Your team's tools or process change with little warning and no clear rationale given.
options: Resist and keep using the old way as long as possible.
Adapt quickly, and ask questions to understand the rationale if it's unclear.
Comply passively without engaging with the reasoning.

change-readiness-mcq-2.scenario: A colleague is struggling to adjust to a recent organizational change.
options: Let them work through it on their own.
Proactively help them adjust, sharing what's worked for you.
Point out that the change was inevitable and they should just accept it.

career-readiness-mcq-1.scenario: You're offered a stretch opportunity outside your comfort zone with real risk of struggling publicly.
options: Decline to avoid the risk of visible failure.
Take it, and be deliberate about closing the specific gaps it will expose.
Take it without any specific preparation.

career-readiness-mcq-2.scenario: You realize your current skill set may not support the role you actually want in two years.
options: Assume it will work itself out over time.
Identify the specific gap now and start closing it deliberately.
Wait until a performance review flags it.

executive-readiness-mcq-1.scenario: A decision you need to make will negatively affect one team while benefiting the organization overall.
options: Avoid making the call and let it resolve itself.
Make the call, and communicate the tradeoff and reasoning directly to the affected team.
Make the call without addressing it with the affected team.

executive-readiness-mcq-2.scenario: You need buy-in from a peer group you have no formal authority over.
options: Escalate to get authority to force the decision.
Build the case and relationships needed to influence the outcome without formal authority.
Give up on getting buy-in and act unilaterally within your own scope.

leadership-open-1.scenario: Every leader eventually has to make a call that isn't popular.
leadership-open-1.prompt: Describe a real or hypothetical situation where you had to make an unpopular decision you believed was right. What did you do, and how did you handle the reaction from others?

ai-literacy-open-1.scenario: Working fluency with AI shows up in the judgment calls around using it, not just knowing it exists.
ai-literacy-open-1.prompt: Describe a specific time you used an AI tool for real work. What did it get right, what did you have to fix or verify yourself, and how did you decide when to trust it?

digital-skills-open-1.scenario: New tools show up faster than formal training ever will.
digital-skills-open-1.prompt: Describe a time you had to learn a new tool or technology quickly for work. What was your approach, and how did you know when you were ready to rely on it?

emotional-intelligence-open-1.scenario: Reading a room often matters more than what's actually said in it.
emotional-intelligence-open-1.prompt: Describe a situation where you had to read an emotional dynamic that wasn't being said out loud. What did you notice, and how did you respond?

personality-open-1.scenario: Working style isn't right or wrong, but it is worth knowing about yourself.
personality-open-1.prompt: Describe your natural working style in a fast-changing environment — what energizes you, and what tends to drain you?

communication-open-1.scenario: Explaining something well means adjusting to the listener, not just the content.
communication-open-1.prompt: Describe a time you had to explain something complicated to someone with very different context than you. How did you adjust your explanation, and how did you know it landed?

learning-agility-open-1.scenario: How you handle unfamiliar territory is a better signal than what you already know.
learning-agility-open-1.prompt: Describe a time you had to pick up a new skill or domain quickly. What was your process, and what did you do differently the next time you faced something unfamiliar?

strategic-thinking-open-1.scenario: Strategic tradeoffs rarely have a clean answer.
strategic-thinking-open-1.prompt: Describe a decision you made that required weighing a short-term benefit against a longer-term consequence. What factors did you weigh, and what did you decide?

problem-solving-open-1.scenario: The difference between a real fix and a surface fix usually shows up later.
problem-solving-open-1.prompt: Walk through a genuinely hard problem you solved. How did you break it down, and how did you know you'd found the real cause rather than a surface fix?

critical-thinking-open-1.scenario: Changing your mind under evidence is harder than it sounds.
critical-thinking-open-1.prompt: Describe a time you changed your mind about something important after encountering evidence that contradicted your initial view. What made you reconsider?

creativity-open-1.scenario: Original ideas usually come from somewhere specific, not out of nowhere.
creativity-open-1.prompt: Describe an original idea you generated that others found unexpected or useful. Where did the idea actually come from?

time-management-open-1.scenario: A demanding week reveals what someone actually prioritizes, not what they say they prioritize.
time-management-open-1.prompt: Describe how you planned a particularly demanding week. What got prioritized, what got cut or delayed, and why?

resilience-open-1.scenario: Recovery from a setback says more than the setback itself.
resilience-open-1.prompt: Describe a real setback you experienced at work. How did you recover, and what changed in how you approached things afterward?

change-readiness-open-1.scenario: The first few weeks of an unwanted change usually show the most.
change-readiness-open-1.prompt: Describe a significant change at work that you didn't choose. How did you respond in the first few weeks, and how did that response evolve?

career-readiness-open-1.scenario: Intentional career planning starts with naming the actual gap.
career-readiness-open-1.prompt: Describe where you want to be in your career in a few years, and the single biggest gap standing between where you are now and that goal.

executive-readiness-open-1.scenario: Organization-wide impact means competing interests rarely all win.
executive-readiness-open-1.prompt: Describe a decision you made or contributed to that affected people or outcomes beyond your immediate team. How did you weigh the competing interests involved?

cross-team-prioritization.title: Cross-Team Prioritization Conflict
cross-team-prioritization.context: You manage a small platform team. Both the Growth team and the Compliance team have urgent requests for your one available senior engineer, Dana, starting Monday. Growth needs Dana for two weeks to ship a checkout change that's projected to add $40K/month in revenue. Compliance needs Dana for the same two weeks to close a data-retention gap flagged in an external audit, with a hard regulatory deadline in three weeks. Both team leads have already escalated to your director, separately, each assuming they'll get Dana. You have one working day before you have to tell both leads your decision.
cross-team-prioritization.prompt: Write out your decision and how you'd communicate it to both team leads. Be specific: what do you decide, what's your reasoning, and what do you actually say to the team lead who doesn't get Dana?

strategic-resource-allocation.title: Strategic Resource Allocation
strategic-resource-allocation.context: You lead a department with a fixed budget for next year, no increase from this year. Three initiatives are competing for the same headcount and budget: (1) a cost-cutting automation project with a clear 18-month payback period, (2) a new product line your CEO has publicly committed to at a recent investor call but which internal data suggests has uncertain demand, and (3) a technical-debt reduction effort your senior engineers say is becoming a retention risk if ignored much longer. You can fully fund at most two of the three at the level each team says they need; partially funding all three risks under-delivering on everything.
strategic-resource-allocation.prompt: Decide how you'd allocate the budget across the three initiatives, and write the rationale you'd present to your leadership team. Name what you're explicitly choosing not to fund (or fund less), and why.

underperforming-product-line.title: The Underperforming Product Line
underperforming-product-line.context: One of your company's three product lines has missed revenue targets for four consecutive quarters and now operates at roughly break-even. It still has a loyal (if shrinking) customer base and represents 15% of total company revenue. Sunsetting it would free up engineering and support headcount for the two growing product lines, but would mean laying off the ~20-person team dedicated to it, and the product's customers have no equivalent alternative from a competitor. The board has asked you, as the executive owner, for a recommendation at next week's meeting.
underperforming-product-line.prompt: Write the recommendation you'd bring to the board: what you'd do with the product line, the financial and people tradeoffs you weighed, and how you'd frame the decision to the team whose roles are affected either way.

createCompanyWorkspaceForm.description: Provisions the workspace and emails the person you name — they sign up with that address and are attached as its admin automatically. You are never a member of it yourself.

workflowAutomation.title: Automations
workflowAutomation.description: Curated automations that connect features you already use — turn each one on or off for your workspace.

hire_to_onboarding.title: New hire onboarding
hire_to_onboarding.description: When a hired candidate joins, automatically give them a short onboarding checklist and email their manager to schedule a 30-day check-in.

low_score_to_reassessment.title: Low assessment score follow-up
low_score_to_reassessment.description: When someone scores below 50 on an assessment, add a task to review the results now and a reminder to retake it in 60 days.

high_potential_to_succession.title: High-potential flag to manager
high_potential_to_succession.description: When someone's Gap Analysis places them in the High Potential zone, email their manager to consider them for succession planning.

exitInterviewsPage.title: Exit Interviews
exitInterviewsPage.description: Record a structured exit interview for every departure, then run AI-assisted trend analysis across them to spot root causes — flight-risk indicators, manager-related turnover, and department patterns. HR-internal only; departed employees never see their own record.
exitInterviewsPage.analysisDescription: AI-assisted pattern detection across all recorded exit interviews — decision support, not an automated conclusion.
